title: DID NUMBERS 5 DESCRIBE AN ABORTION?
paragraphs:
DID NUMBERS 5 DESCRIBE AN ABORTION?
Why Christians Fiercely Disagree About This Passage—and Why One Difficult Hebrew Sentence Changes the Conversation
There is a passage in the Bible that can make Christians on opposite sides of a room reach for the same Bible…and walk away convinced they have read two completely different things.
Numbers 5:11–31.
One person reads it and says, “This is obviously an abortion.”
Another reads exactly the same passage and says, “Absolutely not.”
And somewhere between those two voices sits an uncomfortable question many believers would rather avoid:
What does the Hebrew actually say?
Not what a meme says.
Not what a political slogan says.
Not what somebody’s favorite preacher said.
Not even what we desperately need the passage to say so that an argument becomes easier.
What did Moses actually write?
Because if we really believe Scripture is the Word of God, then Christians should never be frightened by examining Scripture more closely.
Truth does not become weaker when you look at it.
So stay with me.

Because buried inside this disturbing ancient ritual is a Hebrew expression so difficult that respected Bible translations render it very differently—and understanding that difference may completely change the way you have heard Numbers 5 used.
The scene itself is uncomfortable.
A husband suspects his wife has been sexually unfaithful, but there are no witnesses and she has not been caught in the act.
Under Israel's covenant law, the matter is brought before the LORD.
The woman stands before the priest.

Holy water is placed in an earthen vessel. Dust from the floor of the tabernacle is placed into the water. The woman is placed under oath. The words of the curse are written down and washed into the water.
Then she drinks.
If she is innocent, the curse does not condemn her.
If she is guilty, judgment follows.
That much is relatively straightforward.
Then we reach the words that started the modern controversy.
Numbers 5:27 contains this Hebrew expression:
וְצָבְתָה בִטְנָהּ וְנָפְלָה יְרֵכָהּ
Wəṣāḇəṯāh ḇiṭnāh wənāp̄əlāh yərēḵāh.
Very woodenly, the wording is something like:
“Her belly will swell, and her thigh will fall.”
And immediately we have a problem.
That does not sound like ordinary English because the Hebrew itself is difficult.
The word בֶּטֶן — beten can refer to the belly, abdomen, or bodily interior.
The word יָרֵךְ — yarekh ordinarily means thigh, hip, or loin, although in certain contexts it can function euphemistically in connection with the reproductive region.
The verb connected with צבה — tsabah is especially difficult because its occurrence here is unusual.
And נפל — naphal ordinarily carries the basic idea of falling.
So translators have to make interpretive decisions.
That is why one Bible can sound startlingly different from another.
The ESV renders the curse in terms of the woman’s body swelling and her thigh falling away.
The NRSVue uses the language of the womb discharging and uterus dropping.
The NIV makes the interpretation much more explicit and speaks of the womb miscarrying.
That difference is not imaginary.
It is sitting right there in our English Bibles.
And this is exactly where Christians need intellectual humility.

The NIV’s “miscarry” is an interpretive rendering of a difficult Hebrew expression. It should not be treated as though the Hebrew text simply contains the ordinary equivalent of the English sentence, “God causes an abortion.”
It does not.
But the opposite mistake is also possible.
Christians should not pretend that reproductive loss is linguistically impossible simply because that interpretation makes us uncomfortable.

The Hebrew is difficult enough that interpreters have understood the physical judgment in different ways, including reproductive catastrophe, infertility, bodily wasting, genital injury, uterine prolapse, miscarriage, or some combination of these ideas.

Ancient Jewish interpretation also demonstrates that the passage was understood as describing supernatural bodily judgment associated with sexual guilt; it was not simply read as an ordinary medical recipe for terminating pregnancy.
And there is another enormous detail that frequently disappears from online arguments:
Numbers 5 never explicitly tells us that the woman is pregnant.
Read that again.
The accusation is adultery.
Pregnancy is not stated as the prerequisite for the ritual.
There is no command saying, “If a woman becomes pregnant through adultery, terminate the pregnancy.”
There is no identified unborn child in the narrative.
There is no stated gestational stage.
There is no recipe for an abortifacient.
There is holy water, sanctuary dust, an oath, written curses, a grain offering, priestly administration, and judgment explicitly attributed to the covenant curse.

In other words, whatever physical judgment Numbers 5 describes, the text presents its effectiveness as an act of divine judgment—not as a repeatable medical procedure whose natural ingredients reliably cause an abortion.
Dust and water are not presented as the biological mechanism.
God is Judge.
That distinction changes the question.

Because saying, “Numbers 5 may describe pregnancy loss as one possible consequence of divine judgment,” is not the same claim as saying, “Numbers 5 establishes abortion as an Israelite medical practice.”
Those sentences are not interchangeable.
Even if one accepts “miscarriage” as the correct interpretation of the disputed Hebrew, another question remains:
Was there necessarily a pregnancy to miscarry?
Verse 28 makes the issue even more interesting.
If the woman has not defiled herself, she is vindicated and the Hebrew says:
וְנִזְרְעָה זָרַע
Wənizrāʿā zāraʿ.
Literally, something close to:
“She shall be sown with seed.”
The expression points toward fertility—the ability to conceive.
That is one reason many interpreters understand the curse as involving the woman’s reproductive capacity.
But once again, reproductive judgment is not automatically identical to induced abortion.
That distinction is essential.
And yet there is something else Christians should not run away from.
This passage is disturbing.
It comes from an ancient patriarchal society.
A jealous husband initiates the process.
The accused wife undergoes the ordeal.
Modern readers naturally ask difficult questions about power, vulnerability, marriage, sexuality, and justice.
Those questions deserve more than a dismissive sentence.
But there is a detail easily missed when we read the passage only through modern eyes.
The husband does not get to execute his own private judgment.
Suspicion alone does not establish guilt.
He cannot simply declare her guilty because jealousy burns inside him.
The unresolved accusation is brought out of his hands and before the covenant court, ultimately before God.
And if the woman is innocent, the curse does not condemn her.
Her husband’s suspicion does not magically become truth.
That does not remove every difficulty modern readers experience with the passage.
It does, however, prevent us from reducing the ritual to “a husband gets to punish his wife.”
The text places judgment beyond his personal power.
And that should make every Christian stop before turning Numbers 5 into ammunition.
Because sometimes we approach Scripture already carrying the conclusion we want.
Then we search the Bible for sentences that can be recruited into our argument.
We do this with abortion.
We do it with sexuality.
We do it with money.
We do it with politics.
We do it with divorce.
We do it with judgment.
We do it with grace.
And if we are not careful, we stop allowing Scripture to examine us because we are too busy using Scripture to examine everybody else.
Jesus confronted that kind of religious heart.
People could become experts at finding another person’s sin while remaining strangely blind to their own.
That is why the deeper danger surrounding Numbers 5 is not merely mistranslating one Hebrew phrase.
It is approaching God's Word with a verdict already written.
Sometimes we want the Bible to agree with us more than we want Jesus to correct us.
That is a terrifying place for a disciple to live.
Because the Christian confession is not that Scripture belongs to our tribe.
We belong to Christ.
And Christ is not a mascot for an ideology.
He is Lord.
The same Jesus who spoke uncompromisingly about sin moved toward sinners with astonishing mercy.
The same Jesus who called people to repentance welcomed people religious society considered ruined.
The same Jesus who refused to redefine holiness also refused to treat broken human beings as disposable.
Then He went to a cross.
And there the argument becomes personal.
Because eventually every one of us discovers that we are not standing before God as the attorney.
We are standing before God as the accused.
Maybe your scandal was never public.
Maybe nobody discovered the messages.
Maybe nobody knows what happened in that hotel room.
Maybe your church thinks you are strong.
Maybe your family thinks everything is fine.
Maybe the addiction is hidden behind deleted browser history.
Maybe the bitterness is hidden behind worship songs.
Maybe the affair ended years ago, but you still wake up remembering it.
Maybe you were the one betrayed.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Maybe you carry a decision from your past that nobody around you knows about.
Maybe the word “abortion” itself opens a room inside your heart that you have kept locked for years.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that sin does not matter.
The Gospel is the announcement that sin mattered so much that Christ bore judgment to rescue sinners.
At the cross, holiness and mercy do not cancel one another.
They meet.
Jesus does not save us by pretending we are innocent.
He saves guilty people through His own righteousness, His sacrificial death, and His resurrection.
That is why Christianity has something infinitely greater to offer than another shouting match.
Repentance.
Grace.
Forgiveness.
Redemption.
A new life.
You may have done something you cannot undo.
But you are not beyond the reach of the crucified and risen Christ.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
Jesus can redeem what yesterday did to you.
That does not mean consequences disappear.
It does not mean wounds become imaginary.
It does not mean repentance becomes optional.
Grace is not God calling darkness light.
Grace is God entering our darkness and bringing sinners into His light.
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17.
That is the heartbeat behind everything we mean when we say:
Peter knew scandal.
David knew scandal.
The Samaritan woman knew scandal.
The woman caught in adultery knew public shame.
Paul carried the memory of persecuting Christians.
The early church was not assembled from people who had spotless histories.
It was assembled around a spotless Savior.
And perhaps that is why this strange passage in Numbers can ultimately send Christians somewhere more important than an internet argument.
It can remind us that God sees what human beings cannot see.
He knows innocence when people accuse.
He knows guilt when people hide.
He cannot be manipulated by appearances.
And none of us survives His judgment by being better at accusing someone else.
We need mercy.
We need Christ.
So, did Numbers 5 describe an abortion?
The most responsible answer is more careful than either viral slogan.

The disputed Hebrew describes severe bodily and apparently reproductive judgment, but its precise physiological meaning is genuinely debated. Some modern translations understand it as miscarriage; others translate the language more literally or understand a different reproductive catastrophe. The passage never explicitly says the accused woman is pregnant, never commands abortion as a general practice, and presents the outcome as supernatural covenant judgment administered by God rather than as an ordinary human medical procedure.
Therefore Numbers 5 should not be casually flattened into “the Bible gives instructions for abortion.”
But Christians should be equally careful not to claim that miscarriage is an impossible translation of the disputed language.
Faithfulness does not require pretending ambiguity does not exist.
Faithfulness requires refusing to make Scripture say more—or less—than Scripture says.
And maybe somebody reading this needed more than an answer about Hebrew.
Maybe you needed permission to stop hiding.
Jesus already knows.
Every chapter.
Every secret.
Every compromise.
Every wound.
Every night you wish you could erase.
Every person you hurt.
Every person who hurt you.
Every prayer you were ashamed to pray.
And still the Gospel calls:
Come to Christ.
Not because your past is small.
Because His grace is greater.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop defending the thing that is destroying you.
Stop believing shame when it tells you that hiding is safer than surrender.
Bring the scandal into the light of Christ.
There is forgiveness at His cross.
There is cleansing in His blood.
There is resurrection beyond the grave.
There is a new name beyond the accusation.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But you can take one small step out of the darkness.
It is grace.

Numbers 5 is one of those passages people repeatedly encounter stripped of its language and context. Come back when the argument appears again, open the text yourself, and refuse to let slogans do your Bible reading for you.
Supporting Gospel-centered work matters too.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be bought.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
And if this article accomplishes anything worthwhile, may it not merely leave you knowing more about an obscure Hebrew phrase.
May it leave you wanting to know Him.
Because someday the arguments will stop.
The comment sections will disappear.
The platforms will be forgotten.
And every one of us will stand before the God who knows exactly what happened when nobody else was watching.
On that day, your greatest hope will not be that you won the argument.
Your greatest hope will be Jesus.
Your scandal may explain where you have been—but when you surrender it to Christ, it does not get to write the final sentence.
